title: How I Write LinkedIn Posts That Get 100,000+ Views
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: I've written dozens of LinkedIn posts
that have hit 100,000, 500,000, or even
more impressions. You see, over the last
3 years, I built my LinkedIn to 150,000
followers and used that audience to
scale my SaaS to over 8 million in ARR,
and basically all of it came down to one
thing: knowing how to write posts that
people actually wanted to read. Today,
I'm going to show you exactly how I do
it, from finding what to write about to
the first line to the last line, the
whole process, start to finish. Let's
get into it. So, here's the key to
writing viral posts. Most people write
posts for the algorithm, and that's
exactly why they underperform. The
algorithm's only job is to figure out
what your audience wants to read and
show them more of it. So, if you write
to your audience, the algorithm follows.
No matter how the platform changes, to
answer how you would write viral posts
is always the same: make better content.
But, writing for your audience only
works if you're willing to say things
that your audience actually needs to
hear, not things that make you look
good. Most people default to posting
what everyone else posts: wins, polished
takes, and safe opinions, because that
feels comfortable. But, your audience
isn't scrolling through LinkedIn looking
for more of that. They're looking for
someone who actually understands what
they're going through. That's the
difference between content that gets
some engagement and content that spreads
virally. LinkedIn is a professional
network, and most people on it are
trying to look impressive. Nobody wants
to publicly talk about decisions that
blew up or the things that aren't
working. If you're willing to do that,
you're doing something that less than 1%
of creators on the platform can pull
off, and that's what cuts through. The
most effective version of this is
finding what I call the prolific zone.
Mainstream content is just noise. It's
what everyone is already saying. But, if
you go too far in one direction, people
write you off as a complete lunatic. So,
you want to find a take that's
polarizing enough where people who agree
love it, and the people who don't
actually push back. That's where posts
spread the most. My early content about
eliminating BDRs in B2B SaaS landed
there. Most of SaaS was watching their
BDR team stall out, but nobody's willing
to say the model was broken. I wrote
that the predictable revenue model was
born in 2012 and died in 2023. Half the
people reading it agreed completely. The
other half pushed back hard, and that
tension is exactly what made it viral.
Vulnerability works the same way. When I
posted about a layoff at retention.com,
sharing that we'd fallen out of product
market fit and couldn't fix our churn
for 18 months, my exec team told me I
was crazy and that I shouldn't post it.
I posted it anyway, because that level
of honesty resonates with people who are
going through the same thing and have no
one around them who's willing to say it
out loud. If you have investors, you
probably can't go that far, but the
closer you get to saying things you'd
say only to your spouse behind closed
doors, the better your posts will do.
The best LinkedIn posts answer questions
people already have about your niche.
So, before you write anything, go find
those questions. Start with the top two
or three creators in your space. Go
through their best posts from the last
90 days and write down the topics that
got the most engagement in a
spreadsheet. Then, go to Gemini, which
is powered by Google and YouTube search,
and type, "What are the most common
questions people have about" and then
insert your niche. Add those to the
spreadsheet, too. Then, do the same
thing in Reddit. Search for threads in
your space and note what people are
asking. Between those three sources,
you'll have more ideas than you need.
Once you have topics, I recommend you
build a swipe file before you start
[music] writing. Spend 2 hours going
through the best posts in your space and
pull out the hooks, formats, and closes
that stood out to you. In my case, for
hooks, I look at Chris Walker. For
templates, I look at Nigel Thomas. And
for my closes, I just referenced my own
posts. The key here is to take a
structure or architecture of a post that
already works and put your own story or
angle on top of it. And by the way, if
you're putting in the work to grow your
LinkedIn presence and driving traffic to
your site, you should know who's
actually showing up, and that's what
OurB2B does. We identify your anonymous
website visitors at the person level and
send their LinkedIn profiles straight to
your Slack, completely free. You can
install it in under 5 minutes using the
first link in the description. Now, back
to it. The hook is the most important
part of every post. The hook is
everything before the see more button,
and its only job is to make the reader
click see more, nothing else. Not to
summarize the post, not to set up a
list, just to make them want to keep
reading. The way you do this is by
establishing credibility and saying
something bold enough that the reader
has to see what comes next. Write every
hook as if no one has ever heard of you
before, because most people staring at
your post will have no idea who you are.
The most reliable way to build instant
credibility is using specific numbers.
For example, I spoke to 20 CEOs over the
past 30 days. This works because
brokering information from important
people makes you a credible source
before you said anything else. Or,
something I always say, I bootstrapped
20 million ARR in 3 and 1/2 years. Very
few people have done that, and even
fewer have done it so fast, so anyone
reading it immediately wants to know
what I have to say next. LinkedIn
responds to numbers, so I personally use
them in almost every hook I write. Now,
let's talk about the body. Every post
body should do three things in order.
Number one, agitate a specific pain your
audience is feeling, not generically,
but in a way that makes them feel like
you're describing their exact situation.
Number two, you offer a solution or a
new way of framing the problem. And
number three, you close with a clear
takeaway that they can actually do
something with. There's a mini hero's
journey in the space of a few bullet
points, and it's a structure that keeps
people reading all the way through. The
format you use to deliver it is
flexible. I use lists with bullets with
two or three sentences under them most
of the time. Sometimes numbered lists.
Sometimes I write in plain paragraphs.
Now, until you've found your voice and
you're writing comfortably, I would
recommend you lean on other people's
templates. Take a structure that's
working for someone else and apply your
own story to it. Once you've got a feel
for what's working and what people
respond well to, you can drop the
template and just write, but there's no
reason to rush towards that. Let's talk
about the close. Most posts end with
let's continue the conversations in the
comments or some generic question, and
it kills whatever momentum the post had
built. I think a good close is a little
coy and a little clever. It makes the
reader feel something rather than asking
them to do something. One of the closes
I'm proudest of was a post I wrote for
bootstrappers. It ended up with
something like, "The world is hard on
you when you're small. Stay strong. If
you stay in the game long enough, the
odds that you'll hit it big will
skyrocket. Massive success is inside of
you. It just takes time and usually a
little luck. Keep building." Now, that
makes someone feel something. Saying
something like, "What's your take on
bootstrapping?" doesn't make you feel
anything. And here's a pro tip if you're
